To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cAMP signals are transmitted to the nucleus by multiple PKA isoforms, and that the differential expression of PKA isoforms in cortical and cerebellar cells is the basis of the differential ability of the cells to accumulate cAMP-induced nuclear signals.
the type and the localization of cAMP-dependent kinase regulate transmission of cAMP signals to nucleus in cortical and cerebellar neurons.
the type and the localization of the PKA regulatory isoform, RIIβ, regulate the transmission of cAMP signals to nuclei.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of cAMP signal transduction in the central nervous system.
the role of PKA in the brain, and more specifically with the role of the regulatory RIIβ subunit in cortical neurons.
the molecular basis of signal transduction by the cAMP-dependent protein kinase in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the type and localization of PKA isoform determines whether or not cAMP signals can be transmitted to the nucleus.
cAMP signals are differentially transduced in the brain by the different PKA isoforms.
the differential ability of cortical neurons and cerebellar granules cells to transmit c AMP signals to the nucleus is due to their differential expression of RIIβ, RIIα, and AKAP75.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cAMP signals are transmitted to the nucleus by the PKA holoenzyme, which consists of the catalytic subunit, the regulatory subunit RIIβ and an anchor protein AKAP.
the type of PKA (RI or RII) and the localization of the PKA complex (anchored or not anchored) are critical determinants of cAMP signaling to the nucleus.

RIIβ and its anchoring protein AKAP75 are required to transmit cAMP signal into nuclei in cortical cells, whereas RIIα and its anchoring proteins are sufficient to transmit cAMP into nuclei in cerebellar cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the composition of the PKA holoenzyme is a critical determinant of cAMP signaling.
the type of cAMP-dependent PKA and the localization of the catalytic subunits are crucial for cAMP-induced gene expression.
the localization of PKA is critical to its ability to activate transcription.
